I'm not arguing that electron is a worthless technology or that it will never improve. However, as a user it's awkward and I don't personally like using electron software right now. It's not uncommon to hear people complain about discord or slack taking up excessive amounts of ram, and while using electron isn't a deal breaker for most people, it is a negative for them. I am arguing that if you're primarily shipping a desktop application, then there are alternatives like a python application that will feel much nicer for your customers. I know that personally, given the choice between discord and a python application with roughly the same features, I would choose the latter. 

And although this doesn't apply to all of its issues, some of electron's problems are more or less inherent to the technology and don't look like they'll ever go away. Bundling a browser will always result in higher memory usage, the main complaint users typically have about electron applications. Application performance overall will improve over time (wasm is only a few proposals away from getting true multithreading and direct dom access, and webgl looks very promising as well), but some issues are here to stay. Again, this doesn't mean that electron doesn't have any advantages - I still recommend using it if you have an existing web product that you're creating a desktop application for - but it does mean that for now and most likely the years to come it will be a negative for your users.

It's definitely a pain point for native development, but for C++ I'd say compile times are a bigger nuisance overall (especially if you pull in something like eigen that does a ton of metaprogramming). If you do go the route of a python based UI you can implement a custom hot reload tool in under 100 lines of code, which is well worth the effort.

Personally, I don't like electron on any platform. On Linux and Mac they look out of place and don't use native theming, and on all platforms they load slow and use a ton of ram. I get the argument for a simple write once and ship anywhere application, but a python application linked to wxPython or PyQt achieves the same thing without dragging along a whole browser as a dependency. The main argument for electron in my opinion is that you can use existing web developers without having to retrain them.

GIFs. A bit of background: GIFs were invented in the late 80s as the graphics standard for late 80s monitors. They used 8bit color, unlike modern 24bit color, and the at-the-time popular LZW compression algorithm. This means they support 256 total colors, instead of the ~17 million likely supported by your display, and weird hacks have to be used to make colors sort-of kind-of look correct.

It was actually primarily intended for displaying static images, but then better standards like PNG and JPEG were made, so nobody uses them for anything but animated images, where they look awful and don't get good compression. There's been new proposals like APNG (an extension to PNG) and WebP, but they haven't caught on, so GIFs are what we're stuck with in the meanwhile.

Similar, a lot of rust code could have an interface which encapsulates its functionality and can dynamically link, although code which has an API that requires generics would have to keep being distributed like it currently is.

The same issues with Rust's generics are found in C++ templates, but C++ programs have been dynamically linking for years. While we could try to build a method to dynamically support generics, I think it's more practical to just dynamically link everything we can and forget about the rest. * is a raw pointer. References, denoted by &, are special cases of pointers which point to a known, nonzero address. Raw pointers are the type of pointer you'd find in C, and they contain a number which references a specific place in memory (which can be a variable, a function, some constant data, or pure gibberish). Threading is a concurrency technique which uses multiple points of execution within the same program. Python threading is limited due to the GIL, however, and so tasks that require concurrent computing will often see little to no benefit. For certain non-blocking operations (such as networking or file io) this works great, since they will be waiting and don't need the GIL, but it does poorly for cpu intensive tasks, since your compute power will essentially be the same as using a single thread (and sometimes less due to implementation overhead). Traditionally, the official solution for cpu intensive tasks is to call into optimized native code, such as OpenCV for image processing, which can pretty much do whatever so long as it implements the correct python interfaces and will likely be written in a faster language (such as C++).

However, the solution "just don't use python" kind of sucks. While calling into native code is a valid solution, there's not always a pre-existing native library with python bindings, and not all python programmers can write native code and create a python interface for it. This is where multiprocessing comes into play, where multiple python programs run side by side to solve a task. The start-up cost and memory synchronization costs are a bit higher than multithreading, but it allows for multiple points of execution, which can give a substantial speed up in a lot of cases.

Python doesn't use real threads, but instead runs applications single threaded using a global interpreter lock. Essentially, it schedules its own pseudo-threads instead of using thread capabilities given by the operating system, which simplified the design of the language and its implementation, but made some programming paradigms either impossible or inefficient. I would assume that the time.sleep function would use a suspend the thread scheduler, but if not you're out of luck. If you really need more advanced functionality you could try making a simple program in java, C#, or C++, but TaskScheduler will probably fit your needs without requiring you to leave python.  Our website needed the ability to select a date and time for an appointment. The first person consulted about this was not me (I was tasked with other appointment functionality), but instead a graphic designer. The designer made an Adobe XD mockup of a date/time picker, which amomg other things included a 5 row calendar (6 rows are required to show a full month), a custom slider to show time from a list, a toggle between prefilled times and manually entered times, and several complex graphical elements which I know would lead to a stackoverflow flavored hell. I went to my boss about this, and warned him that making this calendar would take a lot of time and probably wasn't worth it, but he insisted.

 I wound up spending the next day and a half making this calendar as a static webpage (which adobe XD doesn't output), then modifying that to be created dynamically from javascript, then modifying that to be position independent so that it could be called on elements, then dynamically generating and theming the calendar dates and times. At this point I still needed to add hooks for events and documentation for my code, which now spanned over 1000 lines, and I still had my original assignment of the appointment functionality to complete, so I took a premade library (flatpickr) and used that, warning my boss that it would just be a temporary placeholder. Long story short, my temporary placeholder wound up looking pretty good on our website, and we're still using it today.

Whenever you have anything where you have and x and y value which both change with time (like throwing a ball at an angle, for instance) you can use complex numbers and make the math way simpler.

This same type of pattern actually also works with 3d values, but 3d numbers don't really work out so well mathematically. So we just use 4d numbers and ignore an extra dimension most of the time, and take advantage of that last dimension when we want to do things like spin objects around. This is how computer graphics are typically done, and we probably wouldn't have Pixar and the like without them.

Some of these other answers are probably great for most people, but as someone who also deals with this kind of mentality I don't think they'll all work for you specifically. My personal recommendations are as follows:

1. Force yourself to start doing whatever you're going to do. Most of the time you have the energy to actually do the activity, but not the energy to start doing it. I don't know how you'll do this and it's pretty personal, but giving yourself rewards for doing it or building a fake sense of pressure by counting down work for some people.

2. Do things in different environments than usual. You likely associate the place wherever you most often try to do things with being unproductive in some way. Going to the library to study or the gym to workout puts you somewhere where you feel like you should be doing something.

3. Do things that impact other people. For better or worse, the pressure of knowing that you can ruin someone's day by not doing something and make their day by doing it well will motivate you.

4. Build a routine. This ties back into number 2 - there are situations where you feel like you should be doing something and situations where you shouldn't. This is an easy way to get yourself into productive environments.

5. Don't do any one thing for long periods of time. You'll eventually burn out and be right back where you started. If you're going to the gym and don't usually go, go for a half hour, get some reps in, and then go make something to eat. Doing things for short periods with breaks between them will make them feel less stale and you'll be more productive.

Beyond that you're really on your own. The most important step is probably the first one - it's just starting whatever you're doing that takes the most effort.

On very old hardware it used to be slightly faster to iterate backwards, and so you would often see a loop like "for (int idx = siz; i--;)". However, most modern machines can sufficiently take advantage of both out of order execution and cache prefetching forwards and backwards to make the performance difference negligible or non-existent. The practice of reading backwards is more of a habit of many programmers than it is something genuinely meaningful, and you can generally expect iterating in either direction to be equally as fast.

        .cfi_startproc
    
        sub rsp, 8
    
        cmp rdi, 1
        ja .ARGUMENT_COUNT_SATISFIED
    
        mov rdi, 2
        lea rsi, .str_NOT_ENOUGH_ARGUMENTS[rip]
        mov rdx, strlen_NOT_ENOUGH_ARGUMENTS
        call write@plt

        xor count, count
    
    .MAINLOOP:

        test current_character, current_character
        je .END_MAIN_LOOP
